title: Send the small lookup table to the data—not the data to the lookup
goal: Recognize when a small-side join can avoid moving a large fact table, and know where Databricks and Snowflake expose different controls.
tag: Certification cycle 5 · focused lesson 3 · join planning
concept:
A stadium has 10,000 ticket scans and one 20-row gate map. It is cheaper to give every scanner a copy of the tiny map than to send all ticket scans to one map.

A broadcast join copies a small relation to workers that hold partitions of the large relation. Each worker joins locally. This can remove a large shuffle, but the copied side must fit comfortably in worker memory.
example: Four workers each hold 2.5 million payment rows. The merchant dimension has 5,000 rows and is 8 MB. Broadcasting sends 8 MB to each worker: 32 MB total. Shuffling both inputs would move the 10-million-row fact side as well. If the “small” side grows to 2 GB, four copies can turn the optimization into memory pressure.

use_case.when: Use small-side join planning when a very large fact table repeatedly enriches from a genuinely small, reusable dimension.
use_case.example: Ten million card events join to 5,000 merchant-risk records before an hourly fraud aggregate.
use_case.decision: First measure compressed and runtime size, freshness, skew, and the physical plan. Broadcast only when the copied side is safely small. On Snowflake, inspect the optimizer's chosen plan rather than looking for a Databricks-style broadcast hint.

practice: Change the dimension size and worker count. Predict copied bytes and whether the dimension is still a safe candidate before revealing the modeled plan.
boundary: The local model uses size arithmetic, not a Spark or Snowflake optimizer. It omits serialization overhead, compression, statistics quality, join type support, skew, cache reuse, spill, network topology, warehouse internals, concurrency, and actual query profiles.

title: A ConcurrentHashMap scan is a moving view—not a snapshot
goal: Use weakly consistent traversal safely and know when a stable snapshot is required.
concept:
A stock clerk walks the aisles while cashiers keep selling items. The clerk can finish the walk without locking the store, but the list may mix moments in time.

ConcurrentHashMap views are weakly consistent. Their iterators do not fail just because updates occur, but a traversal is not an atomic snapshot. It may reflect some concurrent changes and not others.
example: The map starts with A=5 and B=7. While a report traverses, a writer changes A to 4 and adds C=9. The report may show A=5, B=7, C=9: a valid moving view, but not inventory at one instant. That is fine for telemetry; it is unsafe for an exact financial close.

use_case.when: Use weakly consistent traversal for monitoring, diagnostics, caches, and approximate aggregate work that must not stop concurrent writers.
use_case.example: A service exports current per-tenant queue depths while workers add and remove tenants.
use_case.decision: If the consumer needs one instant, copy under an application-level coordination rule or read from a versioned database snapshot. Do not infer snapshot isolation from the absence of ConcurrentModificationException.

practice: Move the writer before or after each read and watch which versions the report can contain.
boundary: The browser and Java trace use a scripted interleaving, not real threads or a complete set of legal outcomes. They omit memory-model details, resize behavior, bulk operations, contention, null restrictions, ordering, and snapshot implementation costs.

title: Shorten the longest dependency chain—not the pile of parallel work
goal: Find the delivery critical path and invest in the work that actually moves the finish date.
concept:
Four checkout lines can finish early while one passport desk keeps the whole trip waiting. Completing more work is not the same as moving the final date.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work. A task on that chain has zero schedule slack in this toy. Speeding a parallel task with slack looks productive but does not shorten delivery.
example: A platform launch has schema design (3 days), migration (5), and consumer cutover (4): 12 days. In parallel, dashboard work takes 6 days. Saving two days on dashboards still leaves a 12-day launch. Saving two days on migration makes the launch 10 days—if no other path becomes longer.

use_case.when: Use critical-path analysis when multiple teams are busy but the release date keeps moving or an executive asks where one senior engineer can change the outcome.
use_case.example: A lakehouse migration has schema, backfill, and consumer validation dependencies plus parallel observability and training work.
use_case.decision: Map real predecessor evidence, include approval and queue time, and recalculate after changes. Do not starve reliability work merely because it has slack; use the model to sequence help, not to declare other work unimportant.

practice: Move two engineering days between migration and dashboard work. Predict the release date and which path becomes critical.
boundary: The model has two deterministic paths and unlimited staffing. Real programs have resource contention, uncertain estimates, rework, cross-path coupling, risk, learning, policy gates, and work that is valuable even when not schedule-critical.

title: Discover MCP capabilities before choosing the modern protocol path
goal: Use server discovery and per-request metadata without assuming every MCP server supports the same protocol era.
concept:
A universal travel adapter checks the outlet before sending power. It does not push one plug into every wall.

In MCP 2026-07-28, a client may call server/discover to learn supported versions and capabilities. The modern core is stateless: version and client capabilities travel in request _meta. Discovery is optional, so a harness still needs an explicit compatibility policy for older servers.
example: The harness prefers 2026-07-28 and needs tools plus tasks. Server A advertises 2026-07-28 and tools, but Tasks are an extension it lacks. The harness can use tools and disable background-task UX. Server B supports the legacy initialization era, so an SDK may fall back if policy permits; a pinned-modern client should fail clearly.

use_case.when: Use discovery when one harness connects to independently upgraded MCP servers or needs to choose modern stateless behavior before ordinary calls.
use_case.example: An enterprise agent connects to catalog, ticketing, and code servers maintained by different teams.
use_case.decision: Pin when compatibility and auditability outweigh reach. Allow an SDK-managed fallback only with tests and telemetry. Always gate optional features on advertised capability and enforced policy, not on a server name.

practice: Switch advertised versions and task support. Watch the harness choose modern, legacy, or fail-closed routes.
boundary: The browser is a capability intersection model. It sends no JSON-RPC, authenticates no server, validates no schemas, implements no fallback transport, and does not prove an extension is safe or authorized.

title: Let light write—and later read—the state of one photonic element
goal: Understand what an all-optical thin-film lithium-niobate memristor demonstrates and what remains a research claim.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · new peer-reviewed research · November 6, 2026
concept:
A whiteboard remembers the last marker stroke without needing a powered screen. A memristive element similarly has a response that depends on prior stimulation.

A newly published Nature Photonics paper reports turning thin-film lithium niobate, an established photonic platform, into an all-optically controlled memristive material. Optical pulses change a state that later light can probe. The claimed integration advantage is avoiding a separate heterogeneous memory material.
example: In the teaching model, three write pulses increase an optical state from 0.20 to 0.65. A later low-power read reports transmission linked to that retained state. The model only explains history dependence; it does not reproduce the paper's material physics, device metrics, wavelength behavior, or reservoir-computing experiment.

use_case.when: Consider this research when studying integrated photonic memory or neuromorphic optical computing where moving state between electronic memory and an optical circuit is costly.
use_case.example: A future photonic reservoir could encode history in waveguide-local elements before a readout stage.
use_case.decision: Treat it as a research direction, not a production component. Evaluate endurance, retention, write/read energy, variability, fabrication yield, array control, and comparison with electronic or heterogeneous alternatives.

practice: Apply positive and negative optical pulses, then use a separate low-strength read and observe the retained state.
boundary: This bounded scalar teaching model is not the experiment. It invents no device performance. It omits photorefractive dynamics, wavelength-dependent bidirectionality, noise, endurance, retention time, fabrication, speed, energy, arrays, and reservoir-computing accuracy.

title: A green workflow is not deployment evidence until the deployment status says so
goal: Model release progress as deployment states tied to an immutable revision, not merely a successful workflow run.
concept:
A courier can finish the delivery route while the recipient still rejects the package. “Route completed” and “package accepted” are different facts.

A GitHub workflow run records automation execution. A deployment records a request for a specific ref, and deployment statuses describe its progress: queued, in progress, success, failure, or error. GitHub does not access your servers; the deployment integration must report the real outcome.
example: Workflow run 812 builds SHA a1b2 and exits zero after asking Argo CD to deploy. The cluster health gate fails five minutes later. If the pipeline marks only the workflow green, the dashboard lies. A deployment for SHA a1b2 should move queued → in_progress → failure with a log URL.

use_case.when: Use deployment records and statuses when release completion is asynchronous or another system actually performs rollout and health checks.
use_case.example: GitHub Actions submits an EKS deployment to Argo CD and waits for health evidence from the cluster.
use_case.decision: Key every deployment to an immutable SHA or digest, publish transitions from the system that observes them, and include logs. A synchronous tiny deployment may report directly, but never equate dispatch success with production success.

practice: Change cluster health after workflow completion and compare workflow state with the deployment timeline.
boundary: The model is an in-memory state machine. It does not call GitHub, Argo CD, EKS, protection rules, environments, webhooks, authentication, retention APIs, concurrency controls, or rollback automation.

title: HTTP 425 says: do not replay this unsafe request in early data
goal: Use 425 Too Early to prevent replay-prone early-data execution without treating every retry as safe.
concept:
An express lane lets a known customer enter before the identity check finishes. That saves time, but a copied entry ticket could be replayed.

TLS early data can arrive before the full handshake completes and is vulnerable to replay. HTTP 425 Too Early tells the client the server refused to risk processing the request early. A user agent that retries should wait for the handshake and send it once normally.
example: A client sends POST /payments as early data. The edge cannot guarantee replay safety, so it returns 425 before calling the payment service. After the handshake, the client retries normally with the same idempotency key. The payment service still needs atomic duplicate protection; 425 only protects this early-data boundary.

use_case.when: Use 425 at an HTTP endpoint or intermediary that accepts TLS early data but cannot safely process a potentially replayed non-idempotent request.
use_case.example: A global edge receives a payment POST in 0-RTT data before the TLS handshake is complete.
use_case.decision: Disable early data for unsafe routes when possible. Otherwise reject early processing with 425 and retry only after handshake completion. Still enforce application idempotency for side effects; never loop-retry another 425 as early data.

practice: Switch between GET and payment POST, with or without early data, and observe whether the request is served, rejected, or needs application duplicate protection.
boundary: The browser models three booleans, not TLS 1.3, a proxy, a real HTTP client, replay windows, caches, anti-replay infrastructure, or payment idempotency storage. Client behavior varies; test your stack.
